title: Influence of the Acoustic Environment in Hospital Wards on Patient Physiological and Psychological Indices
research_question: This study aims to discuss the influence of the acoustic environment on patient physiological/psychological indicators and the mechanism of the effect on recovery using VR technology. Specifically, it investigates: (1) whether the acoustic environment can promote recovery in terms of physiological indicators; (2) whether sounds can decrease or increase the psychological function of patients in hospital wards; and (3) whether demographic factors and other environmental factors will cause different degrees of impact.

participants.description: 70 inpatients (36 men, 34 women) from internal medicine departments of hospitals in Harbin, China, with an average age of 48.2 years (SD = 3.42; min = 18; max = 72). Proportions of participants younger than 45, 45-60, and over 60 years old were similar. Participants had clear cognitive consciousness, sufficient visual, auditory, and behavioral abilities, and stable diet/sleep status. Patients with hyperthyroidism and supraventricular tachycardia were excluded.
participants.recruitment: Inpatients from the internal medicine department of the First Hospital of Harbin and the Second and Fourth Affiliated Hospitals of Harbin Medical University.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A digital three-dimensional (3D) model of a standard single hospital ward (6.6 x 3.6 x 2.8 m, bed size 2.1 × 0.9 m, U-shaped rail curtain, bedside cabinet) was visualized by participants wearing HTC Vive VR glasses. The scene was experienced from the perspective of sitting on the bed.

Four typical sound categories (Mechanical, Artificial, Background/Ambient, Music - 'Day and Night' light music without lyrics) were presented via headphones. Each sound sample was 5 minutes long and adjusted to an equivalent sound pressure level (LAeq) of 50 dB(A). Ambient noise served as a control condition.

mechanisms: Music plays an important role in reducing stress and aiding physiological (skin conduction) and psychological stress recovery.
Artificial sound contains more transient noise, which may negatively impact psychological recovery.
Heart rate is highly sensitive to information processing, which was not involved in this study, leading to an insignificant effect on RHR.
Skin conductance is sensitive to changes in the luminous environment, while heart rate is more responsive to facade patterns.
Acoustic stimuli altered participants' visual cognitive processing, leading to perceived order, comfort, and stimulation.
Patients' acoustic expectations may relieve the negative impact of mechanical noise.
implementation_implications: A hospital's acoustic environment is an important influencing factor on the stress recovery of patients and can serve as a reference for healthcare architects and policy makers.
Hospital wards must provide suitable acoustic environments to help patients relax and recover.
Music plays an important role in reducing stress as it can aid in a patient's physiological (skin conduction levels) and psychological stress recovery.
Mechanical and anthropogenic sounds exert negative effects on a patient's stress recovery.

limitations: VR conditions could draw patients' attention to visual stimuli and weaken the restorative effect of soundscapes.
The music used in this study was not self-selected, and different musical tastes of patients could affect the restorative impact.
The influence of participants' acoustic expectations may explain some results.
The potential function of space (e.g., socializing, working) could influence environmental expectations and evaluations.
Visual stimulation might be a dominating factor affecting environmental appraisal in healthcare settings, potentially diminishing the impact of soundscape.
Physiological data alone may be insufficient to interpret stress levels, as recovery is a complex process involving cognition and reflection.
Future studies could consider patients' social-economic characteristics.
Future work should examine the absolute influence of the acoustic environment in realistic environments.
Future studies could consider other hospital spaces, such as outpatient halls, waiting rooms, double beds, and dormitory bed wards.
